title: Current and long-term liabilities
subtitle: Maturity determines liquidity risk
openingQuestion: A company has a lot of current debt maturing next year but little cash. What is the main risk?
openingOptions: Interest-rate risk, since the borrowing cost gets dearer
Liquidity risk - not enough cash to repay debt on time
explanation: Current liabilities mature within 12 months, so they are obligations that must be settled with real cash, not with a good outlook. A business performing well can still default if a loan comes due at the wrong moment without enough cash gathered and no way to refinance - that's liquidity risk, quite different from a loss risk. That's why reading a balance sheet must also cover the maturity schedule, not just the total outstanding debt.

realWorldExample.description: Masan Group structures its debt across a mix of current (funding working capital) and long-term (plant investment, M&A) - the ratio of current to long-term debt reflects a financing strategy matched to each type of asset.

quiz.question: Current versus long-term liabilities differ by:
options: Scale: under or over one billion dong
Lender: a bank or a supplier
Interest rate: below or above 10%/year
Term: under or over 12 months
quiz.explanation: The classification is based on the time until it must be paid.

quiz.question: A company borrows 1,000 billion over 10 years, paying 100 billion in year 1. How is it recorded?
options: Current 100 billion, long-term 900 billion
The full 1,000 billion recorded as a long-term liability
The full 1,000 billion recorded as a current liability
Current 900 billion, long-term 100 billion (portions swapped)
quiz.explanation: The portion due <12 months = reclassified as current to reflect the true payment pressure.

quiz.question: High long-term debt affects:
options: Inventory turnover
The leverage ratio (D/E)
The dividend payout ratio
Gross margin
quiz.explanation: D/E and the Debt Ratio ↑ = higher leverage = higher risk.

quiz.question: When interest rates rise, a company borrows long-term to:
options: Get a preferential rate the bank only ever offers on long-term loans
Convert current liabilities into equity
Lock in the interest cost, avoiding higher rates later
Reduce the debt-to-equity ratio
quiz.explanation: Long-term borrowing = locking in today's interest rate. If rates rise, the company benefits.

quiz.question: A 20-year bond is classified as:
options: A current liability, since bonds must always be repaid within the year
Not classified
Equity
A long-term liability (matures after 12 months)
quiz.explanation: 20 years = clearly long-term. Only reclassified when the final year (<12 months) approaches.

quiz.question: With high long-term debt, to reduce risk a company should:
options: Improve OCF to raise its ability to repay debt
Pay more dividends to retain shareholders
Borrow more short-term to pay down long-term debt
Buy more fixed assets to increase scale
quiz.explanation: Debt needs to be meaningful: the return earned from it must exceed the interest rate.

quiz.question: Long-term debt rising while OCF falls is a sign of:
options: Normal - these two metrics aren't fundamentally related
Bad - leverage is rising while cash isn't improving
Good - long-term debt helps ease short-term pressure
Good - the company is expanding using borrowed capital
quiz.explanation: Borrowing more while the return earned doesn't rise is the main risk for the company and its investors.

keyTakeaways: Current liabilities: maturity ≤ 12 months - higher liquidity risk
Long-term liabilities: a longer repayment period, usually higher interest
The debt maturity profile is an important repayment schedule to track

practicePrompt.question: Company Z has 800 billion of debt maturing within the next 11 months, while current assets are only 300 billion and expected operating cash flow is 200 billion/year. What is the biggest risk facing this company?
options: Liquidity risk: there may not be enough current assets to cover that debt as it falls due next year
No significant risk since the company is still generating positive operating cash flow every year
The only risk is that market interest rates might rise in the near future
Foreign-exchange risk, because the debt might be denominated in foreign currency
practicePrompt.explanation: Current liabilities (maturity ≤ 12 months) carry higher liquidity risk than long-term ones: even if the company is profitable on the income statement, if current assets (300 billion) and cash flow aren't enough to cover the massive debt coming due (800 billion), the company could face a liquidity crisis or be forced into an urgent debt restructuring.

summary.keyIdea: Current liabilities: maturity ≤ 12 months - higher liquidity risk
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Long-term liabilities: a longer repayment period, usually higher interest

application.title: Classify your own debts by maturity
application.message: If you have a loan or an instalment payment, write down which parts must be settled within the next 12 months and which run longer - this is exactly how a business's balance sheet classifies current versus long-term debt.
application.secondary: Knowing your repayment schedule clearly keeps you from being blindsided when a large debt suddenly comes due.

sections.text: Liabilities are split into current and long-term based on a single criterion: time to maturity. Current liabilities must be paid within 12 months, long-term liabilities have a longer repayment horizon. This classification matters because it determines the liquidity pressure a business faces over the coming year.
Why maturity matters more than the size of the debt

A company with total debt of 1,000 billion but spread evenly over 10 years is far safer than one owing 500 billion that is entirely due next year. In the second case, if the company doesn't have enough cash and can't borrow anew to roll over the debt (refinance), it can fall into a liquidity crisis - even while it's still profitable and its business is still doing fine.
Maturity profile - the full picture of debt

A debt maturity profile is a chart showing how much debt comes due each future year. Credit analysts and bondholders always study this chart closely to spot a 'maturity wall' - a year when a huge amount of debt comes due at once. If that year coincides with a period of tight credit markets (higher interest rates, banks restricting lending), the business can face serious trouble refinancing.

items: Current liabilities: short-term bank loans, the portion of long-term debt due within the next 12 months, bonds close to maturity
Long-term liabilities: long-term bonds, project investment loans, long-term finance leases
Current portion of long-term debt: the part of long-term debt due within the next 12 months, needs to be tracked separately

sections.label: The matching principle in financing
sections.text: Long-term assets (plants, equipment) should be financed with matching long-term capital. Using current liabilities to fund long-term assets creates continual refinancing risk - if credit conditions worsen at the exact moment new financing is needed, even a good project can run into a crisis.

concepts.def: Financial obligations to be paid within 12 months
Financial obligations with a payment horizon beyond 12 months
A chart showing how much debt comes due each year
Borrowing anew to pay off an old debt that's coming due

lines: Maturity determines liquidity pressure, not just the size of the debt.
A maturity wall is a risk to identify early when analysing a highly leveraged business.
The matching principle helps a business avoid unnecessary refinancing risk.
